justification:
Technical round 1 for /oop-design/factory-builder-singleton/. `node tools/run-code.mjs src/content/articles/oop-design/factory-builder-singleton.md` from the issue-111 worktree, run twice consecutively: PASS both times, blocks=20, executed=10, byte-identical result each run, no flakiness (including the Parallel.For/Lazy<T> concurrency sample and both xUnit samples, one of which is an intentionally-failing `fails` block).

All ten runnable samples read for correctness and idiom: the notification simple-factory switch, the Factory-Method ReportExporter/CreateWriter template, the Abstract-Factory Light/DarkWidgetFactory pair (correctly guarantees matched families), the fluent HttpRequestBuilder (validates in Build(), correctly rejects a missing method), the StringBuilder chain, the WebApplicationBuilder file-based-app demo (`#:sdk Microsoft.NET.Sdk.Web` verified against the real file-based-apps directive list - it is listed there as the literal example usage), the Lazy<T> Singleton with ExecutionAndPublication mode, the bad-singleton xUnit test (correctly fails because both OrderProcessor instances share one static EmailSender.Instance), and the AddSingleton/constructor-injection rewrite with its passing xUnit test. All ran clean, no bugs found in any sample. The GoF classification is correct throughout: chapter 3 of Design Patterns is Creational Patterns covering exactly Abstract Factory, Builder, Factory Method, Prototype and Singleton, matching both the article's opening sentence and its later five-pattern list; per the sources list rule for textbooks that cannot be opened online, the book is cited only by chapter, never by page, and no quotation marks are ever placed around Gamma/Helm/Johnson/Vlissides text - the same safe convention already used in strategy-observer-decorator (verified in round 1 of that article) and correctly reused here.

I independently fetched and read six of the article's Microsoft Learn sources (not trusted from the article) and checked every quoted fragment against the live page text. Five check out verbatim: 'By default, all public and protected members of the Lazy<T> class are thread safe and may be used concurrently from multiple threads' (Lazy<T> Thread Safety section, exact); 'Fully thread safe; uses locking to ensure that only one thread initializes the value' (Lazy<T> equivalence table, exact, case-only adaptation); 'each operation that appears to modify a String object actually creates a new string' (StringBuilder Remarks, exact); 'Most of the methods that modify the string in a StringBuilder instance return a reference to that same instance' (StringBuilder Remarks, exact); 'with preconfigured defaults' (WebApplication.CreateBuilder, exact, all three overloads say this); 'Singleton services must be thread safe' (service-lifetimes Singleton section, exact, case-only); 'difficult to unit test' and 'the app should use a mock or stub... which isn't possible with this approach' (dependency-injection/overview, exact, order preserved, ellipsis correctly omits only 'MessageWriter class' mid-sentence). The `#:sdk Microsoft.NET.Sdk.Web` directive and the file-based-apps citation are accurate paraphrase, not a quote, and match the live docs exactly.

Two quotations do not hold up under the same scrutiny (see issues): the StringBuilder-manipulation-cost quote silently changes the source's actual wording while keeping it inside quotation marks, and the service-lifetimes Singleton quote splices two real sentences together in the reverse of their actual order in the source, which is not what an ellipsis is for. Both are hard-rule 'no fabricated/altered quotes' matters even though the underlying claims they support are true and well-documented elsewhere on the same pages - the same category of finding that capped solid-principles' round-1 technical score at 7.0 for one comparable misquotation, and this article has two.

Internal consistency with published siblings is good: the ServiceCollection/AddSingleton/AddTransient/BuildServiceProvider shape matches solid-principles' DIP-vs-DI-container section precisely (same method names, same registration order convention, same `using ServiceProvider provider = ...` disposal pattern), and the 'Gamma, Helm, Johnson and Vlissides catalogue this shape as X, one of the Y patterns' phrasing matches strategy-observer-decorator's citation style verbatim in structure. No contradictions in terminology found.

Depth is strong and differentiated: four GoF patterns are given genuine, distinct runnable demonstrations (not just definitions), the article correctly identifies that the modern fluent-builder shape used everywhere in the BCL and in HttpRequestBuilder is narrower than GoF's original two-role Builder+Director split - a distinction most tutorial-level treatments skip - and the Singleton section goes further than 'here is Lazy<T>' by building a concrete, verified before/after (a real failing xUnit test against a hand-rolled singleton, then the same scenario fixed with AddSingleton + constructor injection). That is a genuinely useful, checkable narrative arc most existing GoF pattern write-ups (refactoring.guru, tutorial sites) do not attempt in C#.

Not higher: two verified quote-integrity problems (one a wording alteration inside quotation marks, one a reversed-order splice) are exactly the kind of finding the technical editor role exists to catch, and the brief treats altered quotations as a hard-rule violation regardless of whether the underlying claim is separately true.

issues.location: 'Builder in the BCL: StringBuilder and WebApplicationBuilder' section, the sentence beginning "`StringBuilder` is the oldest fluent builder in the BCL. Strings are immutable, so..."
issues.problem: The article quotes, in quotation marks and cited to source [[4]] (the StringBuilder Class page): "a routine performs extensive string manipulation". I fetched the live page's Remarks section directly: the actual sentence is "For routines that perform extensive string manipulation (such as apps that modify a string numerous times in a loop), modifying a string repeatedly can exert a significant performance penalty." The article's quoted fragment changes the source's plural "routines that perform" to a singular "a routine performs" while presenting it inside quotation marks as verbatim. The phrase as quoted does not appear anywhere on the cited page. The underlying claim (extensive string manipulation is costly, which is why StringBuilder exists) is true and is the page's own point, but the specific wording attributed to Microsoft is not Microsoft's wording.
issues.fixLooksLike: Either quote the source exactly - e.g. "...which the documentation says exerts 'a significant performance penalty' for 'routines that perform extensive string manipulation'" - or drop the quotation marks and state it as paraphrase in the article's own words.

issues.location: 'The DI lifetime that replaced it' section, opening sentence "Microsoft's own guidance for the DI container is direct about the fix: ..."
issues.problem: The article quotes, joined by an ellipsis and cited to source [[3]] (Service lifetimes page): "don't implement the singleton design pattern and provide code to dispose of the singleton... if the app requires singleton behavior, allow the service container to manage the service's lifetime". Both halves are individually verbatim, but the live page's Singleton section states them in the opposite order: "If the app requires singleton behavior, allow the service container to manage the service's lifetime. Don't implement the singleton design pattern and provide code to dispose of the singleton." An ellipsis conventionally signals omitted material while preserving the source's order; here it joins two sentences in reverse order, which misrepresents how the source actually reasons from condition to guidance.
issues.fixLooksLike: Quote the two clauses in the source's actual order (condition first, prohibition second), or keep only one clause as a direct quotation and paraphrase the other in the article's own words.

issues.location: 'Singleton, implemented correctly' section, the paragraph beginning "Twenty parallel tasks all read `AppConfiguration.Instance`"
issues.problem: The `lazy-singleton` sample proves single-instance construction two ways: `TimesConstructed` via `Interlocked.Increment` (rigorous - a real atomic counter incremented once inside the constructor) and `hashes.Distinct().Count()` over `GetHashCode()` values collected from 20 parallel accesses (used as the headline 'distinct instances observed: 1' line). `Object.GetHashCode()` is not documented or guaranteed by the BCL to be unique per live instance - two distinct objects are not guaranteed to produce different hash codes - so on its own this check is suggestive rather than a proof of single-instance identity, even though in practice on the current CLR it will not collide for a run of 20 objects. This is not a bug (the article's actual, load-bearing proof is the Interlocked-counter check next to it), just an imprecise piece of supporting evidence for a page that is otherwise careful to distinguish measured fact from assumption.
issues.fixLooksLike: Either note in passing that the hash-code check is a convenient proxy rather than a formal identity guarantee, or replace it with a stronger direct check, e.g. collecting the `AppConfiguration` references themselves into a `ConcurrentBag<AppConfiguration>` and counting distinct references with `ReferenceEqualityComparer.Instance`.
